overview: Each service generates 128-bit UUIDv7 locally (timestamp + randomness). No coordination at all.
limitations: UUIDv7 is 128-bit with probabilistic uniqueness. It does not satisfy the prompt’s strict 64-bit globally unique numeric-ID contract. This is a comparison alternative only when those constraints are relaxed.

estimation.assumption: UUIDv7 uses a 128-bit identifier rather than the required 64-bit integer.
estimation.calculation: 128 / 8 = 16 bytes per raw UUID, versus 8 bytes for a 64-bit ID.
estimation.result: No namespace coordinator is required, but collision probability is nonzero.
estimation.implication: Use only if the width and strict uniqueness requirements can be relaxed; never truncate a UUID to 64 bits.

components.purpose: User-facing caller for unique id generator.
components.rationale: Keep validation and durable state in services; retry only according to the API contract.

components.purpose: Distribute incoming connections across healthy instances for unique id generator.
components.rationale: Health checks and routing policy support scale-out; connection-based systems need compatible session routing.
Keep request handlers stateless where possible; the datastore or a fenced owner enforces concurrency invariants.

components.purpose: Each node generates a 128-bit UUIDv7 with a millisecond timestamp and cryptographic randomness. Optional monotonic sequence handles same-ms bursts and clock regressions locally. No worker ID assignment: uniqueness is probabilistic, not guaranteed. This alternative violates the strict 64-bit requirement.
components.rationale: Document bit width, time ordering, clock behavior, sequence limits and namespace reuse.

entityDetails.purpose: Ephemeral local UUIDv7 generator state, not a durable database entity.
accessPatterns: Generate a UUID using time and cryptographic randomness.
constraints: 128-bit output and probabilistic uniqueness; never truncate to claim compliance with a strict 64-bit contract.

apiDetails.purpose: Generate a bounded batch of unique IDs.
apiDetails.rationale: Serialize 64-bit integers as strings in JSON. Library mode calls this locally; UUIDv7 returns 128-bit values and requires a relaxed ID-width requirement.

buildSteps.title: Callers
buildSteps.explanation: In Design, add Web Client and name it “Callers”. Place it in the leftmost caller/background lane. User-facing caller for unique id generator. Keep validation and durable state in services; retry only according to the API contract. Apply the configuration below and add the listed connections once both ends exist.

buildSteps.title: LB
buildSteps.explanation: In Design, add Load Balancer and name it “LB”. Place it in column 2, row 1 of the HLD; its callers are Callers. Apply the configuration below and add the listed connections once both ends exist.

buildSteps.explanation: In Design, add ID Generator and name it “Local UUIDv7 generators”. Place it in column 4, row 1 of the HLD; its callers are Order Service. Each node generates a 128-bit UUIDv7 with a millisecond timestamp and cryptographic randomness. Optional monotonic sequence handles same-ms bursts and clock regressions locally. No worker ID assignment: uniqueness is probabilistic, not guaranteed. This alternative violates the strict 64-bit requirement. Document bit width, time ordering, clock behavior, sequence limits and namespace reuse. Apply the configuration below and add the listed connections once both ends exist.

steps.title: Callers → LB → Order Service → Local UUIDv7 generators
steps.explanation: The diagram represents a local library boundary: combine timestamp and cryptographic randomness, optionally a monotonic same-ms sequence. There is no coordinator call.

steps.title: Order Service → Local UUIDv7 generators
steps.explanation: UUIDv7 produces 128-bit identifiers and probabilistic uniqueness. Choose this only after relaxing the strict 64-bit numeric-ID requirement; truncation breaks its guarantees.

failureCases.scenario: Clock moves backward or a worker lease is reassigned
failureCases.handling: A Snowflake generator stops/waits rather than emitting overlapping timestamps; fence obsolete leases and delay namespace reuse. Ticket ranges avoid clock dependence but lose global time order.

alternatives: Use Snowflake for strict 64-bit roughly time-ordered IDs with disciplined leases and clocks. Use ticket ranges if creation-time order can be relaxed. Use UUIDv7 only if 128-bit width and probabilistic uniqueness are acceptable.
